claims.text: Service-relevant thermal histories such as slow cooling or HIP promote formation of a secondary phase in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The thermally induced secondary phase can segregate preferentially to grain boundaries.
The secondary phase is brittle.
Secondary-phase formation reduces dislocation mobility.
Grain-boundary segregation of the secondary phase localizes stress at grain boundaries.
Secondary-phase formation and grain-boundary stress localization cause a loss of toughness and a shift toward brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous single-phase, typically BCC, high-entropy alloy.
Rapid cooling retains the single-phase structure, whereas slow cooling or HIP permits secondary-phase precipitation.
The secondary phase may be HCP, Laves, or another intermetallic phase within the original matrix.
Thermal exposure causes a precipitation reaction or eutectoid decomposition.
A grain-boundary secondary phase acts as a preferential site for crack initiation and propagation.
Slow cooling or HIP increases hardness relative to the single-phase baseline.
Slow cooling or HIP reduces tensile elongation relative to the single-phase baseline.
Slow-cooled or HIP-treated samples exhibit intergranular fracture features indicative of brittle failure.
Samples that remain single-phase maintain higher toughness and ductile fracture modes.
The as-cast or rapidly cooled single-phase baseline has good toughness.
The proposed behavior is applicable to room-temperature loading and high-temperature creep when thermal exposure is sufficient to trigger phase transformation.
The exact identity of the secondary phase and its quantitative toughness effect may vary with alloy composition and processing.
A controlled comparison should use samples of identical composition processed either by rapid cooling or by slow cooling/HIP.
Failure to detect a secondary phase together with statistically similar fracture behavior in both processing groups would falsify the proposed precipitation-mediated toughness-loss hypothesis.
